displayQuote: The greatest victory is that which requires no battle

meta.title: Who really said "The greatest victory is that which requires no battle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line is a modern paraphrase of Sun Tzu’s Art of War (ch. 3). Giles’ 1910 text reads “breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The greatest victory is that which requires no battle'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Sun Tzu in spirit, but a modern paraphrase in wording. The Art of War ch. 3 actually reads “breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.”

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 544 – c. 496 BC · reputed author of The Art of War
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Sun Tzu’s — it compresses chapter 3 of The Art of War, where the highest skill is to defeat an enemy without fighting — but this exact wording is a modern English paraphrase, not a line found in Lionel Giles’ or other standard translations.

source.heading: The passage it paraphrases
source.excerpt: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting. … Thus the highest form of generalship is to balk the enemy’s plans; … the worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities.
trail: The genuine passage — “supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting” — is chapter 3 of the Giles translation of The Art of War ↗.
The same wording is corroborated in the Marxists Internet Archive copy of Giles’ chapter 3 ↗; neither text contains the popular sentence.
The popular wording is nonetheless circulated as a verbatim Sun Tzu line, e.g. on Goodreads, credited to “Sun Tzu, The Art of War” ↗.
A scan of the 1910 Giles first edition ↗ lets you read the original chapter 3 in full.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner is a modern compression of this
source.excerptNote: Lionel Giles’ 1910 translation of chapter 3. Other renderings run “to subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill.” None of the standard translations use the popular sentence verbatim.

sourceLink.text: The Art of War, chapter 3 (Giles translation)

source.rightsNote: The Art of War is ancient and Giles’ 1910 translation is public domain. The popular paraphrase itself is a modern, anonymous rewording of that public-domain text and carries no known separate rights holder.

author.heading: Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: c. 544 – c. 496 BC · Chinese general and strategist
author.bio: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) was a Chinese general, strategist, and philosopher traditionally placed in the late Spring and Autumn period. He is the reputed author of The Art of War, a thirteen-chapter treatise that has shaped military, political, and business thinking for more than two millennia. Its third chapter, Attack by Stratagem, argues that the highest skill is to subdue an enemy without fighting at all — the idea the popular line compresses.

misattribution.heading: A real idea, but not his real words
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — the thought is authentically Sun Tzu. The problem is authenticity of wording: the polished one-liner is circulated as if it were a verbatim line from the text, when it is a modern paraphrase.

items.scope: Quoted as a verbatim line from
items.why: No standard translation contains the sentence. Giles’ chapter 3 reads “supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting” (full text ↗); other editions render it “to subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill.”

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is genuinely Sun Tzu’s — chapter 3 of The Art of War ↗ makes exactly this argument — but “the greatest victory is that which requires no battle” is a modern English paraphrase, not a sentence he wrote.

context.heading: Winning without fighting
lead: Chapter 3 of The Art of War ranks the ways to prevail. Defeating an enemy in open battle, Sun Tzu argues, is not the highest skill; the true masterpiece is to break an opponent’s will and plans so completely that no fighting is needed. The popular quote distills that whole argument into eight words.

Because the compression is so faithful, it has spread everywhere — strategy books, business talks, social media — usually inside quotation marks as if lifted straight from the treatise. It is better understood as a modern rendering of a genuine ancient idea than as a direct citation.
detailsBody: Translations diverge sharply here. Lionel Giles (1910) uses “supreme excellence” and “breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting”; Samuel B. Griffith’s 1963 version popularized “to subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill.” The smooth “greatest victory / no battle” phrasing matches neither — a sign it originated as a paraphrase rather than a specific edition.
